# Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models

Tobias Cord-Landwehr, Christoph Boeddeker, Reinhold Haeb-Umbach
Affiliation: Paderborn University, Communications Engineering
Department, Paderborn, Germany

###### Abstract

We propose an approach for simultaneous diarization and separation of
meeting data. It consists of a complex Angular Central Gaussian Mixture
Model (cACGMM) for speech source separation, and a von-Mises-Fisher
Mixture Model (vMFMM) for diarization in a joint statistical framework.
Through the integration, both spatial and spectral information are
exploited for diarization and separation. We also develop a method for
counting the number of active speakers in a segment of a meeting to
support block-wise processing. While the total number of speakers in a
meeting may be known, it is usually not known on a per-segment level.
With the proposed speaker counting, joint diarization and source
separation can be done segment-by-segment, and the permutation problem
across segments is solved, thus allowing for block-online processing in
the future. Experimental results on the LibriCSS meeting corpus show
that the integrated approach outperforms a cascaded approach of
diarization and speech enhancement in terms of WER, both on a
per-segment and on a per-meeting level.

###### Index Terms: 

diarization, source separation, mixture model, meeting

## I Introduction

Meeting transcription can be divided into three tasks: Diarization,
which provides the annotation about who spoke when, and which consists
of the subtasks segmentation and speaker identification; separation and
enhancement which is about improving the quality and/or intelligibility
of the speech signals; and finally automatic speech recognition (ASR),
the actual transformation of the speech into written text. Earlier works
mainly focused on optimizing a single of these components to construct a
modular pipeline, e.g. by solely focusing on the separation of
overlapping speech or the diarization of meetings \[[1](#bib.bib1),
[2](#bib.bib2)\]. Recent works consider the complete pipeline as a
holistic system \[[3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4)\], where all steps are
viewed as a single entity.

A wide-spread approach in meeting processing is Guided Source Separation
(GSS) \[[5](#bib.bib5)\]. First, diarization is performed on a meeting.
In essence, any system ranging from embedding-based systems using
d-vectors \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] or x-vectors \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], over
neural speaker diarization systems \[[8](#bib.bib8)\] to multi-stage
systems like TS-VAD \[[9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)\] can be used for
diarization. This diarization is then used as a guide for an
utterance-wise speech enhancement for the speech detected by the
diarization. To this end, a spatial mixture model that enhances the
intelligibility and audio quality is employed for each utterance
individually. While GSS allows for a robust speech enhancement and is
employed in state-of-the-art systems \[[11](#bib.bib11),
[10](#bib.bib10), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)\] it builds upon
previously detected segments and is unable to compensate for missed
speech segments and speaker confusions. Thus, diarization errors are
propagated to subsequent processing stages due to the cascaded nature of
the pipeline structure. Other approaches are based on foregoing the
guide and directly employing a complex Angular Central Gaussian Mixture
Model (cACGMM), the underlying statistical mixture model of GSS, for
speech enhancement \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], or using a neural network-based
approach also for the speech enhancement \[[15](#bib.bib15),
[16](#bib.bib16)\]. However, the statistical mixture-model-based
approaches depend on accurate initialization and knowledge about the
number of active sources. Neural-network-based approaches like TS-SEP
\[[15](#bib.bib15)\] aim to refine an initial diarization estimate but
require in-domain training data.

In this work, we propose a model-based approach by integrating two
models using spectral and spatial features for the diarization and
separation components. This is achieved by incorporating statistical
mixture models designed for each task into a common statistical model
that can be jointly fitted and optimized to the data. Here, a
von-Mises-Fisher Mixture Model (vMFMM) and a cACGMM are integrated into
a common statistical mixture model, the von-Mises-Fisher complex Angular
Central Gaussian Mixture Model (vMFcACGMM). The vMFMM utilizes
frame-level speaker embeddings to perform a diarization by grouping
closely related speaker embeddings into the same cluster. The cACGMM
uses multi-channel STFT features to perform source separation and speech
enhancement based on spatial cues by estimating the speech presence
masks of each speaker. The mixture models are coupled through their
posterior probabilities so that the integrated model can exploit
inter-dependencies between spectral and spatial cues in this way. In
addition, the speaker embeddings ease block-wise processing, as these
speaker embeddings allow the re-identification of speakers between
processed segments and can be used for speaker counting in each
processed segment.

A related work is \[[17](#bib.bib17)\] which also developed a joint
spatial and spectral mixture model, however for the integration of two
source separation models for short recordings. Compared to this, the
proposed approach also encompasses diarization and source counting for
the processing of meeting data.

This work is structured as follows. First,
[Section II](#S2 "II Mixture Model-based meeting processing ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models")
briefly describes how statistical mixture models and the
Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm are applied for meeting data
processing. In particular, a cACGMM-based source separation and a
vMFMM-based diarization system are explained.
[Section III](#S3 "III Integration of separation and diarization ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models")
then explains, how both statistical mixture models are combined into a
common integrated approach. Also, an approach for speaker counting
utilizing the spectral diarization model is motivated. In
[Section IV](#S4 "IV Experiments ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models"),
the integrated model is evaluated against other meeting transcription
models on the LibriCSS database in terms of segment- and meeting-level
transcription performance.

## II Mixture Model-based meeting processing

We propose an integration of diarization and separation by modeling them
with a joint spectral and spatial mixture model. Then, the EM algorithm
is used for joint estimation of the parameters.

In general, the EM algorithm aims to infer latent, unobservable
variables $`\mathcal{Z}`$ from a set of observations $`\mathcal{X}`$.
For mixture models, the complete likelihood function of the observations
is assumed to be the weighted product of $`K`$ distributions

|     |                                                                                                                                                     |     |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Z};\mathbf{\Theta})=\prod_{n}\prod_{k}\left(\pi_{k}p(\mathbf{x}_{n};\Theta_{k})\right)^{z_{k,n}},`$ |     | (1) |

where the weight $`\pi_{k}`$ is the a prior probability $`p(z_{k,n})`$
of the hidden categorically distributed variable $`z_{k,n}\in[0,1]`$
denoting whether an observation $`n`$ is drawn from mixture component
$`k`$ \[[18](#bib.bib18)\]. The EM algorithm works by alternately
estimating the posterior probability
$`{\gamma_{k,n}=\mathrm{E}[z_{k,n}|\mathbf{x}_{n};\mathbf{\Theta}]}`$ in
the Expectation step (E-step) and then optimizing the model parameters
$`\mathbf{\Theta}`$ to maximize the likelihood in the Maximization step
(M-step).

For application in meeting processing, each active source is modeled by
a mixture component. For instance, these components can represent
speakers or positions in a room. Then, the mixture model is fit to the
observations to estimate $`z_{k,n}`$.

### II-A Spatial source separation model

The complex Angular Central Gaussian Mixture Model (cACGMM)
\[[19](#bib.bib19)\] is a statistical mixture model for source
separation utilizing spatial cues. The input features are
$`C`$-dimensional microphone array observations $`\mathbf{y}_{t,f}`$ in
the STFT domain, where $`t`$ and $`f`$ are the time frame and frequency
bin index, respectively. After normalizing the observation to unit
length, these normalized observations $`\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{t,f}`$ are
assumed to be distributed as a mixture of complex Angular Central
Gaussian distributions

|     |                                             |                                                                                                                                                                              |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\_{t,f} | z*{k,t,f}{=}1;\mathbf{B}*{k,f})=\frac{(C-1)!}{2\pi^{C}\det{\mathbf{B}_{k,f}}}\frac{1}{\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{t,f}^{\mathrm{H}}\mathbf{B}_{k,f}^{-1}\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{t,f}},`$ |     | (2) |

which model the spatial cues through the frequency-dependent, spatial
covariance matrices $`\mathbf{B}_{k,f}`$. After convergence, the result
of the last E-step, the component posterior probabilities
$`{\gamma^{\mathrm{spat}}_{k,t,f}=\mathrm{E}[z_{k,t,f}|\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{t,f};\mathbf{\Theta}^{\mathrm{spat}}]}`$
can be interpreted as time-frequency masks for each active source.
Typically, these masks are used to perform mask-based beamforming
\[[20](#bib.bib20)\].

### II-B Spectral diarization model

For diarization, a single-channel von-Mises-Fisher Mixture Model (vMFMM)
using frame-level speaker embeddings as proposed in \[[21](#bib.bib21)\]
is used. First, a frame-level speaker embedding extractor is applied to
the first microphone channel of the observation to obtain the speaker
embeddings $`\mathbf{e}_{t}`$. Whether two embeddings represent the same
speaker is determined by the angle between the embeddings. So, the
length-normalized speaker embeddings $`\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{t}`$ that lie
on an $`E`$-dimensional hypersphere are used as observations for the
spectral mixture model. Therefore, the von-Mises-Fisher distribution
\[[22](#bib.bib22)\]

|     |                                           |                                                                                    |                                                                                                              |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle p(\tilde{\mathbf{e}}\_{t} | z*{k,t}{=}1;\varkappa*{k},\bm{\mu}\_{k})`$                                         | $`\displaystyle=c_{E}(\varkappa_{k})\exp\{{\varkappa_{k}\bm{\mu}_{k}^{\mathrm{T}}\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{t}}\}`$ |     | (3) |
|     | $`\displaystyle c_{E}(\varkappa_{k})`$    | $`\displaystyle=\frac{\varkappa_{k}^{E/2-1}}{(2\pi)^{E/2}I_{E/2}(\varkappa_{k})}`$ |                                                                                                              | (4) |

with the regular first-order Bessel function $`I_{E/2}(\cdot)`$ of
degree $`E/2`$ can be used to model the distribution of frame-level
speaker embeddings for each speaker $`k`$ in a meeting. Each mixture
component is described by its orientation, which can be seen as an
average speaker embedding, $`\bm{\mu}_{k}`$, and its concentration on
the hypersphere $`\varkappa_{k}`$ in order to represent a single
speaker. After convergence, the posterior probabilities
$`\gamma^{\mathrm{spec}}_{k,t}=\mathrm{E}[z_{k,t}|\mathbf{e}_{t},\bm{\Theta}_{\mathrm{spec}}]`$
denoting the probability of speaker $`k`$ being active in a time frame
$`t`$, can be used as a diarization estimate after smoothing and
thresholding.

Fig. 1: Graphical model of the integrated mixture model. The spectral
diarization model (left) and the spatial speech enhancement model
(right) are coupled through the common latent state $`z`$.

## III Integration of separation and diarization

While both models can be individually applied to meeting data, they both
suffer from drawbacks. The cACGMM only handles spatial cues, so nearby
speakers can be confused and the model can split a single speaker into
multiple mixture components due to strong reflections in the room
\[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. On the other hand, the vMFMM has been shown to
mainly achieve a good diarization performance for single-speaker
regions. For overlapping speech, the mixture model needs to be carefully
tuned to represent multiple active speakers, at all. This is crucial
since this approach actually violates the sparsity assumption in
[Eq. 1](#S2.E1 "In II Mixture Model-based meeting processing ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models"):
The latent variable can no longer be assumed to be categorically
distributed if a frame-level embedding $`\mathbf{e}_{t}`$ is to
represent the mixture of multiple speakers. To mitigate these
weaknesses, the spatial cACGMM and spectral vMFMM are integrated into a
common mixture model by coupling them through the latent variable
$`z_{k,t,f}`$. As in \[[17](#bib.bib17)\], this is done by assuming
conditional statistical independence

|                             |                                                                               |                                                               |     |     |
| --------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- | --- |
|                             | $`\displaystyle\begin{split}p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{t,f},\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{t} | z*{k,t,f}{=}1;\mathbf{B}*{k,f},\varkappa*{k},\bm{\mu}*{k})=\\ |
| p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\_{t,f} | z*{k,t,f}{=}1;\mathbf{B}*{k,f})p(\tilde{\mathbf{e}}\_{t}                      | z*{k,t,f}{=}1;\varkappa*{k},\bm{\mu}\_{k})\end{split}`$       |     |     | (5) |

between spectral and spatial variables. To do so, the von-Mises-Fisher
distribution is replicated along the frequency axis, as this axis is
newly introduced for the spectral model. The graphical model of the
integrated mixture model is given in
[Fig. 1](#S2.F1 "In II-B Spectral diarization model ‣ II Mixture Model-based meeting processing ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models").
Using the independence assumption results in the log-likelihood

|                                                                                                                                         |                                                                                                                                                        |     |     |     |
| --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- | --- |
|                                                                                                                                         | $`\displaystyle\begin{split}\ell(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{t,f},\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{t};\mathbf{\Theta})&=\sum*{t}\sum*{f}\sum*{k}z*{k,t,f}(\ln(\pi\_{k,t})\\ |
| \phantom{=}+&\ln(p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{t,f};\mathbf{B}_{k,f}))+\ln(p(\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{t};\varkappa_{k},\bm{\mu}\_{k})))\end{split}`$ |                                                                                                                                                        |     | (6) |

for the integrated model according to
[Eq. 1](#S2.E1 "In II Mixture Model-based meeting processing ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models").
As proposed in \[[23](#bib.bib23), [14](#bib.bib14)\], the a-priori
probabilities $`\pi_{k,t}`$ of each component are set
frequency-independent, but time-dependent which allows to model a
time-varying speech presence probability of each speaker. In the E-step,
the latent variable $`z_{k,t,f}`$ is replaced with its expected value

|     |                                                                            |                                                          |                                                                                                               |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\gamma*{k,t,f}{=}\frac{\pi*{k,t}p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}\_{t,f} | z*{k,t,f}{=}1;\mathbf{B}*{k,f})p(\tilde{\mathbf{e}}\_{t} | z*{k,t,f}{=}1;\varkappa*{k},\bm{\mu}_{k})}{\sum\limits_{\tilde{k}}\pi*{\tilde{k},t}p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}*{t,f} | z*{\tilde{k},t,f}{=}1;\mathbf{B}*{\tilde{k},f})p(\tilde{\mathbf{e}}\_{t} | z*{\tilde{k},t,f}{=}1;\varkappa*{\tilde{k}},\bm{\mu}\_{\tilde{k}})}.`$ |     | (7) |

After replacing $`z_{k,t,f}`$ with its estimate $`\gamma_{k,t,f}`$ in
the log-likelihood (resulting in the auxiliary function $`Q(\cdot)`$),
the parameters of the mixture components are updated to maximize the
log-likelihood during the M-step. This results in an unchanged update
formulation compared to the individual models because the gradients

|     |                                                        |                                                                                                                                                   |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{\Theta}_{\mathrm{spat}}}Q`$ | $`\displaystyle=\nabla_{\bm{\Theta}_{\mathrm{spat}}}\sum_{t}\sum_{f}\sum_{k}\gamma_{k,t,f}\ln(p(\tilde{\mathbf{y}}_{tf};\mathbf{B}_{k,f}))`$      |     | (8) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{\Theta}_{\mathrm{spec}}}Q`$ | $`\displaystyle=\nabla_{\bm{\Theta}_{\mathrm{spec}}}\sum_{t}\sum_{k}\bar{\gamma}_{k,t}\ln(p(\tilde{\mathbf{e}}_{t};\varkappa_{k},\bm{\mu}_{k}))`$ |     | (9) |

w.r.t. the mixture model parameters for the spatial model
$`\bm{\Theta}_{\mathrm{spat}}`$ and spectral model
$`\bm{\Theta}_{\mathrm{spec}}`$ are independent of each other and the
update equations from \[[22](#bib.bib22)\] and \[[24](#bib.bib24)\] can
be used. Here, $`\bar{\gamma}_{k,t}`$ is the sum of the posteriors
$`\gamma_{k,t,f}`$ over all frequencies, which is used as the expected
value of the latent variable during the M-step of the vMFMM.

From these derivations, it can be seen that integrating the vMFMM with
the cACGMM into the vMFcACGMM aims to compensate for the weaknesses of
the individual models. First, spectral cues are introduced without
complicating the individual update equations of either mixture model
compared to a cACGMM-based speech enhancement. Second, the availability
of a frequency dimension in the spectral model eases the detection of
more than one concurrent speaker, improving its capability to handle
overlapping speech. This is achieved since by averaging over the
frequency components, the class posteriors used for the vMFMM parameter
update depict a linear combination of all active classes in a time
frame.

### III-A Embedding-based component fusion & speaker counting

When dividing a meeting into segments to reduce memory and processing
latency, or to account for moving sources, the number of active speakers
in a segment is usually unknown, even if the total number of
participants in a meeting is known. Not only needs the number of
speakers in a segment be estimated, also the assignment of speakers
between the segments, the segment permutation problem, must be solved to
re-identify speakers in different segments.

Integrating the cACGMM with the vMFMM allows for an easy component
fusion. Each mixture component $`k`$ of the integrated vMFcACGMM is
specified by its spatial cues represented in $`\mathbf{B}_{k,f}`$, and
the spectral cues in terms of its spread of speaker embeddings
$`\varkappa_{k}`$ and the average orientation $`\bm{\mu}_{k}`$. This
average orientation can also be interpreted as a prototype speaker
embedding of the mixture component. Therefore, the component fusion can
be designed similarly to the objective of speaker verification
\[[25](#bib.bib25)\]. By comparing the cosine similarity of all mixture
components’ average orientation, superfluous components can be detected,
and split speakers can be merged. First, all pairwise cosine
similarities $`s_{ij}`$ between all mixture components $`i,j`$ are
computed. If any similarities exceed the fusion threshold
$`s_{ij}>\tau`$, the two mixture components with the highest similarity
are fused before continuing the EM algorithm. During fusion, the
posterior probabilities $`\gamma`$ of the two components are combined.
The cACGMM additionally requires the spatial covariance matrix of the
previous step for optimization \[[24](#bib.bib24)\], so the new value

|     |                                   |                                                                                                                                                                               |     |      |
| --- | --------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | ---- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\gamma_{i,t,f}`$   | $`\displaystyle=\gamma_{i,t,f}+\gamma_{j,t,f}`$                                                                                                                               |     | (10) |
|     | $`\displaystyle\mathbf{B}_{i,f}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbf{B}_{i,f}\frac{\sum_{t}\pi_{i,t}}{\sum_{t}\pi_{i,t}+\sum_{t}\pi_{j,t}}+\mathbf{B}_{j,f}\frac{\sum_{t}\pi_{j,t}}{\sum_{t}\pi_{i,t}+\sum_{t}\pi_{j,t}}`$ |     | (11) |

is calculated as the weighted average of the fused mixture components
and the mixture component $`j`$ is deleted afterwards.

## IV Experiments

### IV-A Evaluation Setup

All models are evaluated on the LibriCSS database \[[1](#bib.bib1)\],
which consists of re-recordings of simulated meetings using LibriSpeech
data with $`0\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}40\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ overlap. Here,
results of both a segment-wise and a meeting-wise processing are
reported, where segments are determined by speech pauses as specified in
\[[1](#bib.bib1)\], ranging from
$`30\text{\,}\mathrm{s}60\text{\,}\mathrm{s}`$ on average, while the
full meeting is $`10\text{\,}\min`$ long. Results are given in terms of
Concatenated minimum-Permutation Word Error Rate (cpWER) using the
MeetEval toolkit \[[26](#bib.bib26)\].

The observations $`\mathbf{y}_{t,f}`$ of the spatial mixture model
consist of all $`7`$ microphone channels, transformed into the STFT
domain with an STFT size of $`64\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}`$, a window size of
$`50\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}`$, and a frame advance of
$`16\text{\,}\mathrm{ms}`$, respectively. For the frame-level embeddings
$`\mathbf{e}_{t}`$ of the spectral model, the embedding extractor from
\[[27](#bib.bib27)\] is used, which is trained on partially overlapping
speech mixtures and outputs $`64`$-dimensional speaker embeddings with a
frame-level resolution. This embedding extractor is trained in a
teacher-student fashion, such that the frame-level embeddings aim to
replicate ordinary speaker embeddings. The embedding extractor is
trained using VoxCeleb mixtures, so no in-domain data from LibriSpeech
or LibriCSS is used during the training phase. For embedding-based
component fusion (spectral), a threshold of $`\tau=0.7`$ is chosen, for
the intersection-over-union-ratio-based fusion (IoU)
\[[14](#bib.bib14)\], a threshold of $`\tau=0.85`$ is chosen.

All models use WPE \[[28](#bib.bib28)\] for preprocessing and a wMPDR
beamformer \[[29](#bib.bib29)\] for speech extraction to match the
experimental setup in \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]. To ensure convergence, the
mixture models are fitted for $`100`$ EM steps. Afterward, the priors
$`\pi_{k,t}`$ are smoothed and used to detect individual utterances of
each speaker, serving as the diarization estimate. The detected
utterances are then beamformed and transcribed. For Automatic Speech
Recognition (ASR), the ESPnet model from \[[30](#bib.bib30)\] and the
Nemo ASR model \[[31](#bib.bib31)\] are used.

### IV-B Mixture model initialization

The vMFMM from \[[27](#bib.bib27)\] which serves as the spectral part of
the vMFcACGMM is used to initialize the mixture model. First, an
energy-based Voice Activity Detection (VAD) using minimum statistics is
applied to the recording. Then, the initialization, i.e. the diarization
model, is run only on the voiced segments. A k-Means clustering
\[[32](#bib.bib32)\] is applied to the frame-level embeddings
$`\mathbf{e}_{t}`$ to obtain initial clusters. Then, these clusters are
used as initialization of a vMFMM, which is fitted for $`30`$ iterations
to the data. Here, the maximal concentration of each mixture component
is limited to $`\varkappa_{\mathrm{max}}=35`$, which was shown to offer
a good trade-off between accuracy and capability for overlap detection
in \[[27](#bib.bib27)\]. Afterward, all silence regions detected by the
VAD are set active in an additional noise component. The posterior
probabilities of this mixture model represent the soft-decision
diarization estimates which are used as initial values for the
integrated vMFcACGMM. To this end, the initialization values are
replicated across the frequency axis and set as initial values for
$`\gamma_{k,t,f}`$. The EM-algorithm is started with an M-step to obtain
the initial model parameters.

For evaluation, a global initialization (VMF global) by using the
diarization from \[[27](#bib.bib27)\] to initialize each segment, and an
initialization per segment (VMF) with $`K`$ components per segment is
compared.

TABLE I: cpWER of the vMFcACGMM on LibriCSS segments compared to only
using a cACGMM as spatial mixture model. Models marked with \* assume
knowledge of the number of active speakers per segment.

### IV-C Segment-level Results

First, the integrated vMFcACGMM is compared to only using a spectral or
spatial mixture model, on the LibriCSS segments. This evaluation only
considers the Word Error Rate (WER) on each LibriCSS segment, containing
$`30\text{\,}\mathrm{s}60\text{\,}\mathrm{s}`$, without taking into
account any segment permutation problems.
[Table I](#S4.T1 "In IV-B Mixture model initialization ‣ IV Experiments ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models")
shows that only using the vMFMM diarization (row $`1`$) to initialize a
cACGMM (row $`2`$) leads to high WERs. This is mainly due to diarization
errors leading to missed speakers and multiple mixture components
collapsing to the same speaker. A component fusion based on the
intersection of component priors (IoU) as done in \[[14](#bib.bib14)\]
proves unable to compensate for these errors. If the number of speakers
in a segment is known, a careful initialization of the cACGMM combined
with the IoU-based fusion can be designed to obtain a good WER (row
$`3`$). Compared to row $`2`$, using the frame-level speaker embeddings
for a spectral component fusion already helps to significantly improve
the performance compared to the prior-based fusion (row $`5`$). The
vMFcACGMM then additionally improves upon this (row $`6`$). This shows
that the additional availability of spectral information is beneficial
for the mixture model. By initializing the mixture model
segment-by-segment instead of using the diarization estimate of the
whole meeting, the performance can be further improved (rows $`79`$).
Here, starting the EM iterations with a number of components $`K`$ equal
to or above the total number of speakers in the meeting and using the
spectral component fusion of
[Section III-A](#S3.SS1 "III-A Embedding-based component fusion & speaker counting ‣ III Integration of separation and diarization ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models"),
the WER reduces to $`6.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ (ESPnet, rows
$`7`$/$`8`$). If the total number of classes is used as a stopping
criterion for the fusion (row $`9`$), a WER of
$`5.8\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ is achieved, outperforming the cACGMM from
\[[14](#bib.bib14)\] and reducing the gap to using an oracle diarization
as initialization (row $`10`$).

### IV-D Speaker counting performance

The vMFcACGMM tries to automatically infer the number of active speakers
in a segment according to the embedding-based component fusion specified
in
[Section III-A](#S3.SS1 "III-A Embedding-based component fusion & speaker counting ‣ III Integration of separation and diarization ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models").
[Figure 2](#S4.F2 "In IV-D Speaker counting performance ‣ IV Experiments ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models")
shows that while the mixture model can determine the active speakers
correctly with an accuracy of $`84\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$, i.e. $`596`$
out of $`725`$ segments, the errors mainly occur in segments with more
than $`3`$ active speakers. Here, mainly low-activity speakers that
completely intersect with other speakers are wrongly detected or merged,
so that the $`16\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ speaker errors only contribute
$`1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ to the total WER (compare ESPnet rows
$`8`$/$`9`$). Therefore, the embedding-based component fusion poses an
efficient and simple speaker counting.

Fig. 2: Speaker counting accuracy of the vMFcACGMM in
[Table I](#S4.T1 "In IV-B Mixture model initialization ‣ IV Experiments ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models"),
row $`7`$

### IV-E Comparison of segment-level and meeting-level results

While the total number of speakers in a meeting can be assumed to be
known, the number of active speakers within a short segment of the
meeting will hardly be known. Contrary to the cACGMM, the vMFcACGMM
directly allows for segment-wise processing of meetings, because it can
robustly estimate the number of speakers. Further, the speaker
prototypes $`\bm{\mu}_{k}`$ allow solving the segment permutation
problem: After applying the model to each segment, a simple k-Means
clustering is performed on the prototypes to align the segment-level
results and compare them against other systems that perform a
transcription for the whole meeting, i.e. the full
$`10\text{\,}\mathrm{min}`$.
[Table II](#S4.T2 "In IV-E Comparison of segment-level and meeting-level results ‣ IV Experiments ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models")
shows, that using the integrated model from
[Table I](#S4.T1 "In IV-B Mixture model initialization ‣ IV Experiments ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models"),
row $`8`$ and using the speaker prototypes for segment alignment
($`\bm{\mu}`$)
([Table II](#S4.T2 "In IV-E Comparison of segment-level and meeting-level results ‣ IV Experiments ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models"),
row $`5`$), significantly outperforms a cascaded approach of diarization
followed by Guided Source Separation (GSS) (row $`1`$). Even with
subsequent embedding extraction and Segment Level Reassignment (SLR)
\[[33](#bib.bib33)\] (row $`2`$), this cascaded approach cannot approach
the integrated model.

| 2   | VMF $`\rightarrow`$ GSS \[[33](#bib.bib33)\]   | –        | SLR          | $`10.6`$ | $`9.6`$  |
| 3   | VMF $`\rightarrow`$ cACGMM                     | $`14.7`$ | SLR          | $`13.9`$ | $`13.3`$ |
| 4   | VMFcACGMM                                      | $`5.7`$  | SLR          | $`6.2`$  | $`5.4`$  |
| 5   | VMFcACGMM                                      | $`5.7`$  | $`\bm{\mu}`$ | $`6.7`$  | $`5.4`$  |
| 6   | VMFcACGMM $`\rightarrow`$ GSS                  | –        | $`\bm{\mu}`$ | $`5.5`$  | $`4.7`$  |
| 7   | TS-SEP $`\rightarrow`$ GSS\[[15](#bib.bib15)\] | –        | –            | $`5.6`$  | $`3.5`$  |

TABLE II: Comparison of cpWER on LibriCSS segments and the full meetings
after aligning the segments. Oracle denotes the meeting WER for an
oracle alignment of the speaker permutation across utterances. All
configurations use the Nemo ASR model.

Compared to the neural network-based TS-SEP pipeline (row $`7`$/$`8`$),
the vMFcACGMM loses by more than $`1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ absolute even
without SLR and an additional GSS postprocessing (row $`6`$) only serves
to reduce the difference. However, TS-VAD and its extension TS-SEP
heavily rely on large amounts of in-domain training data, as was
experienced in a CHiME-7 submission \[[34](#bib.bib34)\]. There, only
limited in-domain training data was available, and TS-VAD performed
poorly compared to its performance on LibriCSS. On the contrary, the
vMFcACGMM is a strong meeting processing system that can be applied
without access to neither in-domain nor paired, i.e. corrupted and
clean, training data. For comparison, a TS-SEP system designed for
LibriCSS can not be directly used on the DipCo meeting corpus
\[[35](#bib.bib35)\], a subset of the CHiME-7/8 challenge. To our
knowledge, all CHiME challenge participants required training on the
DipCo data to design a working system, whereas the vMFcACGMM from
[Table II](#S4.T2 "In IV-E Comparison of segment-level and meeting-level results ‣ IV Experiments ‣ Simultaneous Diarization and Separation of Meetings through the Integration of Statistical Mixture Models")
achieves a cpWER of $`52.1\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ without modification or
fine-tuning. This is on par with the CHiME-8 Nemo baseline system
\[[13](#bib.bib13)\] of $`54.6\text{\,}\mathrm{\%}`$ which heavily
relies on using in-domain training data.

## V Conclusions

In this work, we proposed the integration of two statistical mixture
models for the simultaneous enhancement and diarization of meeting data.
It allows for a robust speech enhancement on meeting segments while at
the same time inferring the number of active speakers. By using the
speaker prototypes of the spectral model to solve the segment
permutation problem, the model allows a segment-by-segment processing of
arbitrarily long meetings. Unlike TS-VAD and other neural network-based
approaches, the proposed system requires neither in-domain nor paired
training data. This is important for in-the-wild meeting transcription,
where domain-specific paired data is unavailable for training. In the
future, we will focus on improving speaker embedding quality, thus
reducing the complexity of speaker counting and segment alignment.
